screens.title: Generics and Iterators
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we learn why Java Generics matter and how iteration tools let you traverse and modify collections safely. Generics let you declare the type a collection will hold so the compiler prevents accidental mixing of types and removes the need for manual casting. Iteration tools range from the concise enhanced for-loop, ideal for read-only processing, to Iterator and ListIterator, which let you remove, add, or replace elements while traversing. Together these features reduce runtime errors like class cast failures and concurrent modification exceptions. You'll see short code demonstrations that start with a non-generic list that can produce a type error, then refactor that example with generics to show compile-time protection. We'll then practice traversal patterns: a simple for-each pattern for reading, an Iterator pattern that safely removes elements, and a ListIterator walkthrough for adding and replacing while moving forward and backward in a list. By the end you'll know which tool to choose when you want safety and which when you need mutation control, and you'll understand the common mistake that causes a concurrent modification exception and how to avoid it.

Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Generics and Iterators
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Generics and Iterators

Understand type-safe collections and safe traversal patterns that prevent common runtime errors in Java.

In this lesson
Why generics prevent type errors.
Coming up
How Iterator and ListIterator let you change lists safely.
Goal
Choose the right traversal for read or mutate operations.
Why this chapter

Generics and iteration are everyday tools for collection processing. They reduce runtime surprises and make code clearer. Practically every Java program that handles lists, maps, or sets benefits from these patterns.

Concept Preview
Generics
Declare the element type for compile-time safety.
Iterator
Traverse and remove safely during iteration.
ListIterator
Add, set, and move backwards in a list.
Key Takeaway

Generics reduce bugs by shifting type errors to compile time. Use Iterators to make safe changes during traversal.

You will also learn to traverse collections using the enhanced for-loop when you only need to read data, and to choose Iterator or ListIterator when you need to remove, add, or replace elements while iterating. Finally, you'll practice a small filtering and modification task that combines these skills: removing elements with an Iterator, and inserting or changing elements with ListIterator. screens.title: What are Generics?
screens.narratorSegment: Generics allow you to parameterize classes, interfaces, and methods with a type placeholder so the compiler enforces what kind of objects a collection may hold. Before generics, a list stored raw Object references and you had to cast values when you retrieved them, which meant a hidden mistake might only appear when that cast failed at runtime. A concrete example is a raw list that accidentally contains a string and an integer. When you later retrieve an element and cast it to string, the program may raise a class cast failure at runtime. Generics fix this by letting you write a declaration that says what type the collection must contain. For example, declaring a list that holds only names signals intent to the compiler which then prevents you from adding the wrong type. A common misconception is that generics change how objects are stored at runtime; in Java they mainly provide compile-time checks and clearer code. The practical payoff is fewer runtime surprises, easier refactoring, and cleaner code that documents intent. Keep in mind this is the fundamental reason modern Java code favors ArrayList over raw ArrayList.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › What are Generics?
Definition

Generics provide type parameters

They let you tell the compiler what type a collection will hold so it can stop invalid additions at compile time rather than at runtime.

Why this matters
  • Eliminates explicit casts when retrieving elements.
  • Catches incorrect additions at compile time, avoiding ClassCastException later.
  • Documents programming intent directly in the type system.
Key Takeaway

Prefer parameterized types for collections to make code safer and clearer.

Concrete example
// Non-generic list can mix types List mixed = new ArrayList(); mixed.add("Alice"); mixed.add(42); Object item = mixed.get(1); // You must cast and risk a runtime error when wrong type is assumed
// With generics, the compiler enforces types List names = new ArrayList<>(); names.add("Alice"); // names.add(42); // Compile-time error: wrong type
Misconception: Generics change runtime storage. Reality: they provide compile-time checks and clearer code without altering how objects are stored at runtime.

screens.title: From raw collections to typed collections
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a simple refactor from a raw collection to a parameterized one and see the safety benefits. Imagine a list that once held mixed objects: strings and integers. If you later expect a string and cast a retrieved value, a wrong type will raise a class cast failure at runtime. Refactoring means declaring the collection with a type parameter so only that type can be added. The compiler then flags incorrect additions immediately. For example, if you change the declaration to a list that holds only names, any attempt to add an integer will be a compile-time error. This reduces debugging time and clarifies intent. A common mistaken belief is that generics add runtime overhead; Java implements generics with type erasure so the runtime footprint is not increased, while you still get compile-time safety. Practically, after you make this change, client code no longer needs casts when pulling elements from the collection. The code panel shows both the non-generic snippet and the refactored version so you can compare what changes and what stays the same. Try to read the compile-time messages in a real editor to see how immediate and helpful they are.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Typed Collections Walkthrough
Code Walkthrough
// Before: non-generic list (can hold any Object) List mixed = new ArrayList(); mixed.add("Apple"); mixed.add(100); // int boxed to Integer Object o = mixed.get(0); // requires cast to use as String // After: generic list with declared element type List fruits = new ArrayList<>(); fruits.add("Apple"); // fruits.add(100); // compile-time error — wrong type String f = fruits.get(0); // no cast needed
Compare the two snippets: the refactor removes the need to cast retrieved elements and prevents the accidental addition of the wrong type. This is most powerful in larger codebases where many modules interact with the same collections.
Practical notes
  • Generics primarily add compile-time checks and clearer APIs.
  • They eliminate class cast risks from collection retrieval code.
  • They make refactoring safer because the compiler enforces consistency.
Common mistake

Mixing raw and parameterized types can reintroduce unchecked warnings — prefer consistently parameterized collections across code.

screens.title: Enhanced for-loop (for-each)
screens.narratorSegment: The enhanced for-loop is a concise form for iterating over arrays and any collection that implements Iterable. It is ideal when you only need to read each element and perform an action, because it hides the iterator boilerplate and makes intent clear. For example, iterating over a list of fruits to print each name is straightforward and avoids indexing errors. The for-each loop internally uses an iterator, but you do not see it; that has consequences: you should not modify the collection while the loop runs because the implicit iterator will detect structural changes and throw a concurrent modification exception. In short, prefer the enhanced for-loop when you perform read-only processing. If you later need to remove elements during traversal, switch to an explicit Iterator so you can call the iterator's remove method. This screen shows a small code example and describes the for-each trade-offs and a short checklist to decide when to use it. Enhanced for-loop (for-each) means use the enhanced for-loop for simple, readable traversal when no collection mutation is needed.. In practical terms, readable traversal for read-only processing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Enhanced for-loop
Pattern
List fruits = new ArrayList<>(); fruits.add("Apple"); fruits.add("Banana"); fruits.add("Cherry"); for (String fruit : fruits) { System.out.println(fruit); }
This loop visits every element and is concise. It is the best choice when you only read or compute results from each element. However, because it uses an implicit iterator, avoid structural modifications while the loop runs; if you do mutate the collection directly, a runtime exception will occur.
Quick checklist
  • Use for-each for readable, read-only traversal.
  • If you need to remove elements, use an explicit Iterator.
  • For indexed access or parallel modifications, consider other approaches.
Misconception

The enhanced for-loop lets you safely remove items by calling the list's remove method inside the loop. In fact, that causes a concurrent modification exception; use the Iterator for removals.

screens.title: Iterator: hasNext, next, remove
screens.narratorSegment: The Iterator interface provides three important capabilities: checking for more elements, retrieving the next element, and safely removing the last returned element. Use iterator. hasNext to see if the traversal can continue, use iterator. next to obtain and advance the traversal, and use iterator. remove to delete the last returned element from the underlying collection. This remove method is special: it's the only supported way to remove an element while iterating, because it keeps the iterator's internal state consistent with the collection and prevents a concurrent modification exception. A concrete example is filtering a list of integers to remove even numbers. The iterator pattern walks the list, asks whether the next item exists, reads it, and if it meets the removal condition, calls remove on the iterator. If you instead called the collection's remove method directly during iteration, the iterator would detect a structural change and throw an exception. This screen shows a small code panel with the numbers example and a short runtime output to make the behavior concrete. Iterator: hasNext, next, remove means use iterator.remove to change the collection during iteration; it updates both the iterator state and the underlying collection safely.. In practical terms, safe removal during traversal. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Iterator: safe removal
Code example
List numbers = new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList(1,2,3,4,5)); Iterator it = numbers.iterator(); while (it.hasNext()) { Integer n = it.next(); if (n % 2 == 0) { it.remove(); // safe removal } } // Expected numbers: [1, 3, 5]
This pattern is reliable for filtering operations because it delegates mutation to the iterator itself. That keeps the iterator consistent and avoids runtime exceptions related to concurrent modifications.
Runtime view
Initial: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] Removed: 2 Removed: 4 Final: [1, 3, 5]
Pro tip

Prefer iterator.remove when deleting during traversal; avoid modifying the collection through its API while an iterator is active.

screens.title: For-each vs Iterator
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between the enhanced for-loop and an explicit Iterator depends on whether you will mutate the collection during traversal. The enhanced for-loop is concise and readable; it is ideal for read-only passes where you simply process or print elements. Because it uses an implicit iterator under the hood, it is not safe to remove or add elements using the collection's methods within the loop. In contrast, an explicit Iterator gives you control: you can call its remove method to delete the current element safely. A practical decision rule is simple: if you only need to read elements, use for-each; if you need to remove elements while traversing, use Iterator. A common misconception is that the for-each loop provides the ability to modify safely; it does not. The comparison panel lists clear decision points and shows a short example of the exact line that causes a concurrent modification exception when you incorrectly call the collection's remove inside a for-each loop. Finish by asking yourself: will I change structure while iterating? If yes, pick Iterator. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › For-each vs Iterator
Enhanced for-loop
Pros: concise, easy to read, less boilerplate. Best for read-only processing. Cons: cannot safely change collection structure while iterating.
Incorrect removal pattern

Removing elements by calling the list's remove method inside a for-each will cause a concurrent modification exception when the loop's implicit iterator detects the change.

Iterator
Pros: explicit control, safe removal via iterator.remove. Cons: slightly more boilerplate but required for structural changes during traversal.
Quick rule

If you change the collection while iterating, use the iterator's methods; otherwise prefer the for-each for clarity.

Decision checklist
I only need to read → Enhanced for-loop
I need to remove safely → Iterator.remove
I need bidirectional moves or add/set → ListIterator

screens.title: ConcurrentModificationException
screens.narratorSegment: A ConcurrentModificationException occurs when the structure of a collection changes while an iterator is active and that change was not made through the iterator's supported mutation methods. The enhanced for-loop uses an implicit iterator behind the scenes. If you call the collection's remove method inside that loop, the iterator's internal state and the collection's state diverge, and the iterator detects the unexpected modification and raises the exception. A concrete example in the assessment shows a for-each loop that tries to remove an element by calling the list's remove method; running that code will typically throw a concurrent modification exception at the point of modification. The remedy is to perform removals through the iterator. remove method or refactor the loop to collect items to remove and perform a separate removal pass. Understanding this exception helps you design safe traversal logic and avoid a class of runtime errors that interrupt program execution. Ask yourself: when I remove or add elements during iteration, am I using the iterator's methods? ConcurrentModificationException means modifying the underlying collection during iteration without using the iterator's mutation methods leads to concurrentmodificationexception.. In practical terms, why modifying the collection directly during iteration fails. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › ConcurrentModificationException
Spot the error
List items = new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList("A","B","C","D")); for (String item : items) { if (item.equals("B")) { items.remove(item); // causes ConcurrentModificationException } }
The removal call modifies the list while the for-each's implicit iterator is active. The safe fix is to use an explicit iterator and call iterator.remove() when the condition matches, or collect elements to remove and remove them after the iteration completes.
Fix
Use an explicit Iterator and call its remove method when you decide to delete the current element. That keeps the iterator and collection in sync.
Learner check

Can you find the line in a for-each loop that leads to the exception? Replace it with iterator.remove and verify the iteration succeeds.

screens.title: ListIterator: bidirectional traversal
screens.narratorSegment: ListIterator extends Iterator with additional capabilities suited to lists. It supports moving backward as well as forward, and it also allows you to replace or insert elements at the current position. The key methods are previous, previousIndex, nextIndex, set, and add. A typical use case is when you need to add a new element immediately after a particular existing element or replace a value encountered during traversal. The provided example with colors demonstrates moving forward, adding a new color after a name, then changing another name with set, and finally iterating backwards to review changes. Common mistakes include trying to call set before any call to next or previous, which has undefined behavior because there is no current element to replace. In practice, use ListIterator when you need fine-grained edits while traversing a list; for simple removals, the regular Iterator suffices. Reflect on when you must step backwards or insert in the middle of a traversal; that's the signal to use ListIterator. ListIterator: bidirectional traversal means use listiterator when you need bidirectional movement or to add and set elements while traversing a list.. In practical terms, add, set, and move backward in a list. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. narration.text: ListIterator extends Iterator with additional capabilities suited to lists. It supports moving backward as well as forward, and it also allows you to replace or insert elements at the current position. The key methods are previous, previousIndex, nextIndex, set, and add. A typical use case is when you need to add a new element immediately after a particular existing element or replace a value encountered during traversal. The provided example with colors demonstrates moving forward, adding a new color after a name, then changing another name with set, and finally iterating backwards to review changes. Common mistakes include trying to call set before any call to next or previous, which has undefined behavior because there is no current element to replace. In practice, use ListIterator when you need fine-grained edits while traversing a list; for simple removals, the regular Iterator suffices. Reflect on when you must step backwards or insert in the middle of a traversal; that's the signal to use ListIterator. List colors = new LinkedList<>(Arrays.asList("Red","Green","Blue")); ListIterator it = colors.listIterator(); it.next(); // past "Red" it.add("Yellow"); // adds after "Red" it.next(); // moves past "Green" it.set("Emerald"); // replaces "Green" // colors: [Red, Yellow, Emerald, Blue] // traverse backward while (it.hasPrevious()) { System.out.println(it.previous()); }

screens.title: Common mistakes and defensive patterns
screens.narratorSegment: This slide collects common mistakes and defensive patterns to help you write robust collection code. First, mixing raw collections and parameterized collections reintroduces unchecked casts; prefer a consistent use of generics across code to keep the compiler helpful. Second, removing or adding elements directly on a collection while an iterator is active triggers a concurrent modification exception; the defensive pattern is to call iterator. remove or to accumulate elements to modify in a separate list and apply changes after the traversal. Third, calling ListIterator. set before a next or previous call is invalid; always ensure the iterator has returned an element before replacing it. Another defensive habit is to choose the simplest tool that meets your needs: if you only read, use the enhanced for-loop; if you change elements, use the appropriate iterator. Finally, when you write utility methods that accept collections, prefer using generics in signatures so callers and implementers get compile-time checks. By adopting these practices you catch more errors earlier and make your intentions explicit to future readers. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we learn why Java Generics matter and how iteration tools let you traverse and modify collections safely. Generics let you declare the type a collection will hold so the compiler prevents accidental mixing of types and removes the need for manual casting. Iteration tools range from the concise enhanced for-loop, ideal for read-only processing, to Iterator and ListIterator, which let you remove, add, or replace elements while traversing. Together these features reduce runtime errors like class cast failures and concurrent modification exceptions. You'll see short code demonstrations that start with a non-generic list that can produce a type error, then refactor that example with generics to show compile-time protection. We'll then practice traversal patterns: a simple for-each pattern for reading, an Iterator pattern that safely removes elements, and a ListIterator walkthrough for adding and replacing while moving forward and backward in a list. By the end you'll know which tool to choose when you want safety and which when you need mutation control, and you'll understand the common mistake that causes a concurrent modification exception and how to avoid it.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain why Generics exist and how they prevent runtime type errors by enforcing element types at compile time. You will be able to declare and use parameterized collection types like lists and maps, and read code that uses angle-bracket notation to indicate element types. You will also learn to traverse collections using the enhanced for-loop when you only need to read data, and to choose Iterator or ListIterator when you need to remove, add, or replace elements while iterating. These traversal tools are important because using the wrong pattern leads to common runtime failures such as a concurrent modification exception. Finally, you'll practice a small filtering and modification task that combines these skills: removing elements with an Iterator, and inserting or changing elements with ListIterator. Each objective includes a short reason why it matters and a simple mnemonic to anchor the behavior.

These objectives turn into practical skills: you will recognize the compiler errors that tell you a list is storing the wrong type, and you will be able to refactor non-generic code into parameterized collections so those errors disappear at compile time. You will practice iterating with the enhanced for-loop to read values and with Iterator when you need to remove elements safely. For lists where you must insert or change elements mid-traversal, you'll use ListIterator and its set and add operations. Each skill matters in everyday coding: type errors that would otherwise only appear at runtime are caught early, and removal done incorrectly during traversal results in a runtime exception that interrupts program flow. As a mnemonic, think 'declare intent, then choose your cursor' — declare what the list holds and then pick the traversal tool that matches whether you only read or also mutate. This chapter includes a short hands-on filtering task that ties these skills together.

Generics allow you to parameterize classes, interfaces, and methods with a type placeholder so the compiler enforces what kind of objects a collection may hold. Before generics, a list stored raw Object references and you had to cast values when you retrieved them, which meant a hidden mistake might only appear when that cast failed at runtime. A concrete example is a raw list that accidentally contains a string and an integer. When you later retrieve an element and cast it to string, the program may raise a class cast failure at runtime. Generics fix this by letting you write a declaration that says what type the collection must contain. For example, declaring a list that holds only names signals intent to the compiler which then prevents you from adding the wrong type. A common misconception is that generics change how objects are stored at runtime; in Java they mainly provide compile-time checks and clearer code. The practical payoff is fewer runtime surprises, easier refactoring, and cleaner code that documents intent. Keep in mind this is the fundamental reason modern Java code favors ArrayList over raw ArrayList.

Let's walk through a simple refactor from a raw collection to a parameterized one and see the safety benefits. Imagine a list that once held mixed objects: strings and integers. If you later expect a string and cast a retrieved value, a wrong type will raise a class cast failure at runtime. Refactoring means declaring the collection with a type parameter so only that type can be added. The compiler then flags incorrect additions immediately. For example, if you change the declaration to a list that holds only names, any attempt to add an integer will be a compile-time error. This reduces debugging time and clarifies intent. A common mistaken belief is that generics add runtime overhead; Java implements generics with type erasure so the runtime footprint is not increased, while you still get compile-time safety. Practically, after you make this change, client code no longer needs casts when pulling elements from the collection. The code panel shows both the non-generic snippet and the refactored version so you can compare what changes and what stays the same. Try to read the compile-time messages in a real editor to see how immediate and helpful they are.

The enhanced for-loop is a concise form for iterating over arrays and any collection that implements Iterable. It is ideal when you only need to read each element and perform an action, because it hides the iterator boilerplate and makes intent clear. For example, iterating over a list of fruits to print each name is straightforward and avoids indexing errors. The for-each loop internally uses an iterator, but you do not see it; that has consequences: you should not modify the collection while the loop runs because the implicit iterator will detect structural changes and throw a concurrent modification exception. In short, prefer the enhanced for-loop when you perform read-only processing. If you later need to remove elements during traversal, switch to an explicit Iterator so you can call the iterator's remove method. This screen shows a small code example and describes the for-each trade-offs and a short checklist to decide when to use it. Enhanced for-loop (for-each) means use the enhanced for-loop for simple, readable traversal when no collection mutation is needed.. In practical terms, readable traversal for read-only processing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The Iterator interface provides three important capabilities: checking for more elements, retrieving the next element, and safely removing the last returned element. Use iterator. hasNext to see if the traversal can continue, use iterator. next to obtain and advance the traversal, and use iterator. remove to delete the last returned element from the underlying collection. This remove method is special: it's the only supported way to remove an element while iterating, because it keeps the iterator's internal state consistent with the collection and prevents a concurrent modification exception. A concrete example is filtering a list of integers to remove even numbers. The iterator pattern walks the list, asks whether the next item exists, reads it, and if it meets the removal condition, calls remove on the iterator. If you instead called the collection's remove method directly during iteration, the iterator would detect a structural change and throw an exception. This screen shows a small code panel with the numbers example and a short runtime output to make the behavior concrete. Iterator: hasNext, next, remove means use iterator.remove to change the collection during iteration; it updates both the iterator state and the underlying collection safely.. In practical terms, safe removal during traversal. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Choosing between the enhanced for-loop and an explicit Iterator depends on whether you will mutate the collection during traversal. The enhanced for-loop is concise and readable; it is ideal for read-only passes where you simply process or print elements. Because it uses an implicit iterator under the hood, it is not safe to remove or add elements using the collection's methods within the loop. In contrast, an explicit Iterator gives you control: you can call its remove method to delete the current element safely. A practical decision rule is simple: if you only need to read elements, use for-each; if you need to remove elements while traversing, use Iterator. A common misconception is that the for-each loop provides the ability to modify safely; it does not. The comparison panel lists clear decision points and shows a short example of the exact line that causes a concurrent modification exception when you incorrectly call the collection's remove inside a for-each loop. Finish by asking yourself: will I change structure while iterating? If yes, pick Iterator. For-each vs Iterator means use enhanced for-loop for read-only tasks; use iterator for safe removal during iteration.. In practical terms, when to use concise reading vs controlled mutation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A ConcurrentModificationException occurs when the structure of a collection changes while an iterator is active and that change was not made through the iterator's supported mutation methods. The enhanced for-loop uses an implicit iterator behind the scenes. Let's summarize the core concepts to remember. First, Generics let you declare the element type of collections so the compiler protects you from adding the wrong type and you no longer need casts when retrieving elements. Second, the enhanced for-loop is a clean and readable pattern for read-only traversals, but it is not safe for structural modifications mid-iteration. Third, Iterator provides explicit traversal control with hasNext, next, and remove; its remove method is the safe, supported way to delete elements while iterating. Fourth, ListIterator extends the iterator for lists with bidirectional movement and methods to set and add elements at the cursor. Finally, avoid mixing raw and parameterized collections and never call collection. remove during an active iterator; use iterator. remove or a post-processing step. These ideas together make collection code safer, easier to read, and less prone to runtime exceptions.
